questions.question: What is a topology $\boldsymbol\tau$ on a set $\boldsymbol X$?
options: A single distance function on $\boldsymbol X$
A collection of subsets of $\boldsymbol X$ satisfying the topology axioms
A finite list of points of $\boldsymbol X$
A collection containing only singleton subsets.

questions.question: Which closure property must a topology $\boldsymbol{\tau}$ satisfy?
options: Arbitrary unions of sets in $\boldsymbol{\tau}$ stay in $\boldsymbol{\tau}$.

questions.question: Which two sets must belong to every topology on $\boldsymbol X$?
For a set $\boldsymbol X$, which collection is the trivial topology described?
options: The collection of all singleton subsets only

questions.question: Which closure property is required for unions in a topology?
options: Only the union of exactly two elements of $\boldsymbol\tau$ is allowed.
Unions of elements of $\boldsymbol\tau$ must never belong to $\boldsymbol\tau$.
Any union of elements of $\boldsymbol\tau$ must belong to $\boldsymbol\tau$.
Only finite unions are allowed, while arbitrary unions are forbidden.

questions.question: Which closure property is required for intersections in a topology?
options: Every infinite intersection of elements of $\boldsymbol\tau$ must belong to $\boldsymbol\tau$.
No intersection of open sets may be open.
The intersection of any finite number of elements of $\boldsymbol\tau$ must belong to $\boldsymbol\tau$.

questions.question: Let $\boldsymbol X = \{a,b\}$. Which collection is a topology on $\boldsymbol X$?
Which collection on $\boldsymbol X = \{a,b\}$ fails to be a topology because it omits $\boldsymbol X$?
Why does the definition mention finite intersections rather than arbitrary intersections?
options: Intersections are never relevant to topologies.
Topologies close under finite, not arbitrary, intersections.
Finite intersections must always be empty.

questions.question: What does the interpretation say a topology allows us to study without using a distance?
A metric space induces a topology by declaring open sets to be unions of open metric balls. Which statement follows?
options: Every metric space can be viewed as a topological space.
No metric space can be a topological space.
Metric spaces have no open sets.
Only finite metric spaces induce topologies.

questions.question: Consider $\boldsymbol\tau = \{\varnothing,\{a\},\{b\},\boldsymbol X\}$ on $\boldsymbol X = \{a,b\}$. Why is this a topology?
options: It omits the empty set but contains enough singletons.
It is a topology only because $\boldsymbol X$ has exactly one element.
It has $\varnothing$, $\boldsymbol X$, and stable unions and finite intersections.

questions.question: What is a topology on a set $X$?
options: A metric with exactly one open ball.
Subsets of $X$ satisfying the topology axioms.
An ordered list of points in $X$

questions.question: Which two sets must belong to every topology $\tau$ on $X$?
Which collection is a topology on $X=\{0,1\}$?
Let $X=\{a,b\}$. Which collection satisfies the mandatory first axiom for a topology?
If $U_i\in\tau$ for every $i$ in some index set, what must also belong to $\tau$?
If $U,V\in\tau$, what does the finite-intersection axiom imply?
Why does a topology generalise metric openness?
options: It requires every open set to be a metric ball.
It specifies open sets without requiring a distance function.

questions.question: Which collection is the discrete topology on $X$?
options: The collection of all finite sequences in $X$
The collection of all subsets of $X$
